title: OpenAI launches MedChemBench: GPT-6.2 Astra scores 84.5% on medicinal chemistry reasoning
summary: Medicinal chemists face the same question every day: which compound to synthesize and test next. OpenAI's new MedChemBench uses 99 problems from published research to test whether AI can connect molecular structure, experimental evidence, and the decision of what to try next. The best performer, GPT-6.2 Astra, earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh setting, but compound selection and numerical prediction remain weak spots.
ai_summary: On November 20, 2026, OpenAI released MedChemBench, a benchmark for medicinal chemistry reasoning. Its 99 problems, drawn from published research, test whether AI can link molecular structure and experimental evidence to the compound to test next. At the shared xhigh setting, the most demanding tier common to all models, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 84.5% overall, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 83.3% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 58.2%. By component, Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures, earning 95.4%, but scored only about half the available credit on compound selection and numerical prediction. For scientists looking to use AI in drug discovery, this helps show where models are strong and weak; OpenAI cautions, though, that it does not mean the models can discover new drugs, prior exposure to public sources cannot be ruled out, and each problem was answered once with no tools.
brief: MedChemBench has 99 problems, drawn from 117 papers and patents and covering 761 distinct molecular structures.
xhigh overall scores: GPT-6.2 Astra 84.5%, GPT-6 Astra 83.3%, GPT-6.1 Sol 82.0%, GPT-5.6 Sol 58.2%.
Astra earned 95.4% on molecular structure reconstruction, but only about half the credit on compound selection and numerical prediction.
On the 18-atom-ring spatial reasoning problem, GPT-6 Astra got all 10 attempts right and the GPT-5.6 models got all 10 wrong.

sections.h: What MedChemBench is: a test of medicinal chemistry reasoning

blocks.p: OpenAI released MedChemBench on November 20, 2026. It is not an AI that finds drugs; it is a suite of evaluation problems designed to see whether models can match what molecules look like with what experiments measure, then decide which compound to try next. Medicinal chemistry is the discipline of designing, modifying, and evaluating compounds for use as medicines.

The hardest part of this work is tradeoffs: improving one property often worsens another. A compound may act strongly on a disease-relevant protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Working medicinal chemists routinely design, synthesize, and test series of closely related compounds, then decide which direction to go next. MedChemBench tests whether AI has that ability to connect structural changes with experimental evidence.

sections.h: What four abilities does it test?

blocks.p: MedChemBench splits scoring into four categories. For most problems, the model sees the context available at a given point in a research program: the biological target, research goals, compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. It is then scored on four dimensions:

list: Molecular structures: correct atom connections and stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
Scientific reasoning: explanations supported by the evidence provided, such as why one compound was chosen over another.
Ranking and selection: compound rankings and choices that match the stated requirements.
Property predictions: agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source literature, including measured and calculated properties.

sections.h: How to read the scores: who scored what

blocks.p: At xhigh, the most demanding reasoning setting shared by all models, the top overall score went to GPT-6.2 Astra with 84.5% of available credit, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 83.3%, GPT-6.1 Sol at 82.0%, GPT-6.1 Terra at 75.1%, and GPT-5.6 Sol at just 58.2%.

blocks.p: That 84.5% means percentage of available credit, not a simple accuracy rate: some problems award partial credit, with more credit for values closer to the measured result. The same model's score also changes with reasoning effort: GPT-6 Astra reached 83.8% at the max setting. Figure 2 in the original post plots nine models and 51 model-by-effort combinations against output tokens; the trend is that more reasoning raises scores, but clear gaps remain between models.

sections.h: A concrete problem: block the target, but also be absorbed and avoid rapid breakdown

blocks.p: One MedChemBench problem draws on research into PRMT5 inhibitors. PRMT5 is a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and earlier experimental results, and must simultaneously predict three properties for three related compounds: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly they are broken down in a liver-enzyme assay.

Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff: compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay. In other words, no single compound won on all three. That is the core difficulty of medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not mean better permeability or slower breakdown.

Scoring checks whether the model reconstructed the molecular structures correctly and how close its predictions are to measured values; closer predictions earn more partial credit. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.

sections.h: Before any reasoning, the model has to draw the molecule correctly

blocks.p: Before discussing properties, a model must identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry, and MedChemBench checks whether models preserve that information when reconstructing the molecule.

One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At xhigh, GPT-6 Astra got all ten responses right, while GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed on all ten. In the examples, GPT-5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, and GPT-5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments. Errors like these change the identity of the molecule being analyzed.

This is also Astra's strongest area: it earned 95.4% of available credit for structure at xhigh. By contrast, compound selection and numerical prediction earned only about half. In other words, the model can see molecules clearly and explain its reasoning, but it still has far to go in choosing the right next compound and nailing down exact values.

list: Whether the MedChemBench problem set and scoring code are fully available for download: the announcement links to the paper but gives no release date or access method.
Whether the benchmark will become an OpenAI product or API: the announcement doesn't say.
How models from other companies perform: OpenAI evaluated only 11 GPT models and did not include external comparisons.
Whether the training data includes these papers and patents: OpenAI says prior exposure to the public sources cannot be ruled out.
Whether these scores reflect real-world drug discovery ability: OpenAI says the results do not establish that models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions.
Whether each question allowed multiple attempts or tools: the announcement says each response was a single attempt with no tools, feedback, or new experiments.

blocks.p: Value: for teams in medicinal chemistry or computational chemistry, or anyone asking whether AI can now help pick compounds, MedChemBench offers a reasonably concrete four-part readout. Molecular structure, scientific reasoning, ranking/selection, and property prediction are scored separately, which is more useful than a single overall number.

Tradeoff: it tests reasoning on historical literature, not real drug-discovery workflows. The problems may have been seen during training, and every answer was a single attempt with no tools. Treating it as proof that AI can replace chemists would overstate it significantly.

list: If you're a medicinal chemist: treat it as a capability map, and pay most attention to the weak spots in selection and property prediction.
If you're on an AI team or building benchmarks: the pattern of strong structure and reasoning but weak selection and prediction is a useful starting point for future improvements and comparisons.
If you only care whether AI will find new drugs soon: the safer conclusion is not yet. These results show reasoning ability improving, not that models can discover new drugs.
